name: Transact-SQL
title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server)

type.text: **Static typing over SQL data types**: Every variable, parameter, and column has a declared type, and a block that violates it fails at parse or bind time
**Table variables and table-valued parameters carry a declared row type**: `DECLARE @t TABLE (...)` and a user-defined table type pass a typed row set between units
**A procedure parameter declares its type and direction**: `@p int OUTPUT` fixes the type and the direction, so a caller binds to a signature
**`DECLARE @name` defaults to NULL (T10)**: A declared variable starts as NULL, so an unassigned variable is valid and propagates NULL into the expression
**NULL comparison needs three-valued logic**: With `ANSI_NULLS ON` (the default, and the only supported setting since SQL Server 2017), `@x = NULL` is unknown, so a check needs `IS NULL`
**`sql_variant` is the one escape hatch**: A column or variable of `sql_variant` holds values of different base types, and every consumer must discover the stored base type at run time

construction.text: **A stored procedure provides modularity with a declared interface**: `CREATE PROCEDURE` names the unit, its parameters, and its result, and can return a status value and OUTPUT parameters
**A view or an inline table-valued function separates consumers from the query**: The exposed relation is stable while its defining query can change
**A table-valued parameter passes a row set without a shared temporary table**: A user-defined table type plus a TVP parameter removes the need for a global temporary table
**Set-based statements compose without a cursor**: `INSERT ... SELECT`, `UPDATE ... FROM`, and `MERGE` express the whole transformation in one statement
**Triggers fire implicitly**: An `AFTER` or `INSTEAD OF` trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run

**Session `SET` options change the meaning of a statement**: `ANSI_NULLS` and `QUOTED_IDENTIFIER` are captured when a stored procedure is created, while `DATEFORMAT` applies when the statement runs, so the same text can parse or convert differently elsewhere

memory.text: **No manual memory management**: The SQL Server buffer pool and the query workspace own the memory, and a batch never names an address
**The server grants memory to a query**: The query's memory grant comes from the server's calculator or the Resource Governor, so the batch does not request bytes
**Buffer pool and `tempdb` behaviour are server configuration**: `max server memory`, the `tempdb` files, and a Resource Governor pool are settings, not batch properties
**A sort or hash can spill to `tempdb`**: An operation whose grant is too small writes to `tempdb`, which costs I/O even though the language hides allocation
**A cursor allocates per fetch**: A row-by-row cursor uses workspace per fetch, so the memory pattern follows the loop

error.text: **`TRY ... CATCH` gives a structured path**: The `CATCH` block runs on error and exposes `ERROR_NUMBER`, `ERROR_MESSAGE`, `ERROR_SEVERITY`, and `ERROR_LINE`
**`THROW` and `RAISERROR` raise with a number and a message**: `THROW 50001, 'msg', 1` carries a number, so a handler can branch on it
**`XACT_STATE()` and `@@TRANCOUNT` tell the handler whether the transaction is committable**: A doomed transaction is detectable inside `CATCH`
**Errors ignored or non-exhaustive (Er3)**: A `CATCH` block that swallows the error, or a skipped `@@ERROR` check, lets the batch continue past the failure
**Errors do not abort the batch by default**: Without `SET XACT_ABORT ON`, a statement error rolls back that statement and the batch continues
**Severity decides whether the caller sees the error**: A low-severity error is informational, so the same statement text can pass a caller by

concurrency.text: **Transactions group statements atomically**: `BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, and `ROLLBACK` make a unit of work commit or abort as one

**Isolation levels are selectable and versioned**: `READ UNCOMMITTED`, `READ COMMITTED` (default), `REPEATABLE READ`, `SNAPSHOT`, and `SERIALIZABLE`, while the database options `READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT` and `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` switch `READ COMMITTED` to row versioning and enable `SNAPSHOT`
**Snapshot isolation removes reader–writer blocking**: With `READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON`, a reader uses row versions and does not block a writer
**Set-based statements reduce explicit locking**: One `UPDATE` moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
**Shared mutable state by default (K2)**: `SET` options, `CONTEXT_INFO`, and a global temporary table `##t` are visible to code the caller did not write
**A locking hint couples the query to the engine's concurrency model**: `WITH (NOLOCK)`, `UPDLOCK`, and `READPAST` are engine-shaped and must agree with the application's lock ordering

platform.text: **Client interfaces are standard**: ODBC, JDBC, OLE DB, and ADO.NET reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol
**Bulk interfaces are documented**: `bcp` and `BULK INSERT` use a documented format, so data exchange is not tied to an application API
**Two implementations exist under separate vendors**: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP ASE share a lineage and a core syntax, but the two diverge, and Microsoft and SAP document them separately
**Azure SQL is the same vendor with a different deployment**: The managed service changes availability, administration, and some features, so code targets a specific surface
**Cannot function outside one vendor (P1)**: The language needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE
**The T-SQL surface is engine-specific**: `TOP`, `IDENTITY`, `GO`, the `sys` catalog views, and the `sp_` procedures are SQL Server features, so a port to another engine is a rewrite

performance.text: **A cost-based optimiser with a plan cache executes a statement**: A procedure's plan can be reused, so the caller does not choose an access path
**A columnstore index and batch mode scan analytically**: `CREATE COLUMNSTORE INDEX` plus batch mode processes a large scan in vectorised batches
**Query Store records plans and regressions**: An operator can see a plan change and force a previous plan
**In-memory OLTP tables are lock-free and memory-optimised**: `MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON` tables and natively compiled procedures remove latch contention
**Parameter sniffing can choose a plan for the wrong input**: A cached plan built for one parameter value can be poor for another
**A plan can regress without a query change**: New statistics, a version upgrade, or a changed data volume can select a worse plan

ecosystem.text: **Tooling is mature and first-party**: SQL Server Management Studio, Azure Data Studio, and `sqlcmd` cover administration and query work
**The market and the hiring pool are large**: SQL Server is widely deployed in Microsoft environments, so documentation, training, and consultants are abundant
**Cloud deployment is a first-party service**: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance run the same engine with a managed administration model
**Proprietary (Ec4)**: The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Microsoft (and, for ASE, from SAP) under licence
**The ASE toolchain is separate from the SQL Server toolchain**: SAP maintains its own documentation, tools, and support, so knowledge does not transfer freely

evolution.text: **The release cadence is regular and active**: SQL Server ships a major release periodically, and Azure SQL receives continuous updates
**A compatibility level keeps old behaviour**: A database at an older compatibility level keeps the older optimiser and syntax behaviour while the engine is upgraded
**The engine leads the standard**: `TRY ... CATCH`, `MERGE`, window functions, and JSON support arrived as engine features, so users get them without waiting for the standard
**A deprecated feature is warned and then removed**: The documentation lists deprecated features, so a removal can require edits even though a compatibility level otherwise preserves older behaviour
**Feature availability differs by edition and deployment**: An Enterprise feature or an Azure-only feature may not exist on a local Standard edition

domain.text: **Excellent fit for transactional and analytical logic in the database**: A stored procedure runs beside the data with a plan and a transaction
**One language spans OLTP and analytics**: Set-based DML, window functions, and a columnstore scan all live in the same language
**The surrounding pipeline is first-party**: Integration Services, the Agent scheduler, and Reporting Services cover the rest of a data workflow
**Domain and vendor lock-in (D1)**: The language exists inside SQL Server or SAP ASE, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
**Procedural row logic reads poorly**: A row-by-row algorithm in a cursor is verbose and slow beside its set-based equivalent
**It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs**: The language assumes a SQL Server database and a set-based workload

learning.text: **Gentle for a SQL developer**: A procedure with `BEGIN ... END`, `TRY ... CATCH`, and `SELECT ... INTO` is readable to anyone who knows SQL
**Documentation and examples are complete**: The Microsoft T-SQL reference documents every statement with examples
**The procedural and the set-based model coexist**: A developer must choose between a cursor and a set-based statement, and the wrong choice shows up as a performance problem
**NULL handling must be learned**: With `ANSI_NULLS ON`, `= NULL` never matches, and a comparison with NULL yields unknown
**Plan and locking behaviour is a separate body of knowledge**: Performance work means reading plans and lock waits rather than syntax
**The SAP ASE dialect diverges in details**: Differences in `GO`, `IDENTITY`, and built-in functions mean knowledge transfers only in part

syntax.text: **Keyword-based and readable**: `SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE` and `BEGIN ... END` read close to English
**A procedure is a readable unit**: The parameter list, the body, and the `RETURN` value are declared in one `CREATE PROCEDURE` statement
**`GO` marks a batch boundary in a script**: The client tool sends the batch, so the boundary is visible in the source
**`SET` options prefix every script**: `SET NOCOUNT ON`, `ANSI_NULLS ON`, and `QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON` are usually written at the top, so the boilerplate grows
**`@` and `@@` distinguish kinds of variable by convention**: A local variable, a parameter, and a global function share the sigil, so a reader distinguishes them by spelling
**Identifier quoting depends on a setting**: `[name]` and `"name"` both quote an identifier, and the second form needs `QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON`

testing.text: **`tSQLt` is the established framework**: An open-source unit-test framework runs test classes with mocked tables and assertions
**`TRY ... CATCH` makes a unit test expressible in the language**: A test procedure asserts and `THROW`s on a mismatch
**A transaction wraps a test and rolls it back**: The database is unchanged after the test
**Error metadata supports an assertion on a failure path**: `ERROR_NUMBER` and `ERROR_MESSAGE` inside `CATCH` let a test check the rejection
**No test framework ships with the toolchain (G1)**: SSMS and sqlcmd provide no assertion or runner, so a suite depends on tSQLt or a hand-rolled harness
**A server-side suite needs a server**: The harness needs a SQL Server instance, so the tests couple to infrastructure

security.text: **`sp_executesql` with parameters removes the injection surface**: `EXEC sp_executesql N'SELECT ... WHERE x = @p', N'@p int', @p = 1` passes the value out of band
**`GRANT`, `DENY`, and `REVOKE` with roles express least privilege**: Access is declared per object, per schema, and per role
**Row-level security limits what a statement can see**: A `SECURITY POLICY` with a predicate function filters rows by the caller's identity
**`EXECUTE AS` makes the effective identity explicit**: A procedure can run as its owner or as a named user
**Known vulnerability/injection (Q3)**: A statement built with `EXEC (@sql)` from concatenated input lets the input become code
**Dynamic SQL and owner-rights execution re-open the risk**: `EXEC` on a built string, `sp_OA*` procedures, and `xp_cmdshell` where enabled defeat parameterisation

tradeoffs: **Logic beside the data is deliberate**: Keeping a rule in the database guarantees it for every writer; the cost is that the rule now deploys and versions with the schema rather than with the application
**A cursor is a deliberate trade for row-by-row work**: It makes a per-row algorithm expressible, at the cost of the set-based model

**Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible query**: `sp_executesql` and `EXEC` reach constructs a static statement cannot name; the cost is that the statement's shape is known only when it runs
**`NOLOCK` trades consistency for concurrency**: A reader that accepts dirty reads avoids blocking
verdict: Transact-SQL's coupling follows its host engine. Stored procedures, views, and table-valued parameters give real modularity, `TRY ... CATCH` gives a structured failure path, and the optimiser, Query Store, columnstore, and in-memory OLTP carry performance work. Main strengths: a mature first-party toolchain, a regular release cadence, and standard client interfaces. Main weaknesses: the language only runs on SQL Server or SAP ASE, the useful surface is engine-specific, NULL starts in every declared variable, an unhandled `CATCH` continues the batch, cursor code paths are slow, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard.

energy.text: Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine's, not the program's.

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The database stores the source text and parses it; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
